title: The Road to the North: the Diamond Monopoly, the Chartered Country, and the Grave in the Matobo Hills
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Vicarage and the Voyage Out

stops.name: Bishop's Stortford, the fifth son of the vicar
stops.date_confidence: attested; the birth date and the parsonage are documented, though the coordinate used by one research lens fell some 700 metres east of St Michael's and has been corrected to the church itself
stops.campa: In the parsonage attached to St Michael's in Church Street, the vicar Francis William Rhodes fathers his fifth son by Louisa Peacock. The boy is christened Cecil John. The household is clerical and crowded. The father preaches without notes and intends his sons for the church or the army. Cecil gets neither Eton nor Winchester; he is sent to the grammar school a few hundred yards from his own front door, marked out among his brothers as the delicate one, the boy whose chest will not stand an English winter. The schoolroom map is already red in places.
suggested_refs: St Michael's Church and vicarage, Church Street, Bishop's Stortford; Bishop's Stortford Grammar School
sources: Robert I. Rotberg, The Founder: Cecil Rhodes and the Pursuit of Power (1988)

stops.name: Southampton, the passage to Natal
stops.date_confidence: the departure in June 1870 is attested, but the port is not fixed: Rotberg gives Southampton, other biographies Plymouth; the pin follows the better attested Southampton and the divergence stands unresolved. One research lens dated the sailing to 1869, which contradicts the arrival of 1 September 1870 and is rejected here
stops.campa: At sixteen, judged too weak in the chest for another English winter, he is put aboard a ship for Natal to join his brother Herbert on a cotton farm. He turns seventeen at sea on the fifth of July. The voyage runs more than two months and he carries a Greek lexicon, a classical dictionary, and his mother's money. Nothing in the sending is imperial. It is a family disposing of a sickly son to a warm colony, the ordinary Victorian remedy for bad lungs. What sends him out of England is a doctor's opinion of a boy's chest.
suggested_refs: Passenger lists of the Union Line mail steamers to Natal, summer 1870
sources: South African History Online, 'Cecil John Rhodes'

stops.name: Port Natal, the landing at Durban
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He lands at Durban on the first of September, into a colony he has never seen, to work land he has never worked. The Surveyor-General Peter Cormac Sutherland takes him in at Pietermaritzburg while he waits for Herbert. Natal is sugar and cotton and a labour question already old. Twenty-three years after this landing a young Gujarati lawyer named Mohandas Gandhi will come ashore at the same harbour on a one-year contract and stay twenty-one. The two men never meet. One will write the franchise law of a colony; the other will spend his South African years litigating against laws like it.
suggested_refs: The Point, Durban harbour, landing place of the Natal mail steamers
sources: South African History Online, 'Cecil John Rhodes'

stops.name: Umkomaas valley, the cotton that fails
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the farm and its failure are attested, the month of his arrival on it is not
stops.campa: He joins Herbert on the cotton lands of the Umkomaas valley and works them through a season. The soil is wrong, the prices are wrong, and the brothers are planters by decision rather than by trade. Cecil keeps the accounts, reads for Oxford in the evenings, and watches the venture fail with the detachment of a man who has already priced it. The venture costs the brothers their capital. What he keeps from it is a distinction between producing a commodity and controlling who is permitted to produce it.
suggested_refs: The Rhodes brothers' cotton lands in the Umkomaas valley, Natal

stops.name: New Rush, the boy buys claims
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: News of diamonds on the Vooruitzigt farm empties Natal of young men. Rhodes rides inland to the New Rush claims, eighteen years old, and finds a canvas town of diggers each scratching at a plot thirty-one feet square. Most of them are gambling. He is not. He buys out the discouraged, rents pumps to the flooded, and begins assembling out of a thousand quarrelling smallholdings the single property a company can own. Within a decade the camp will be called Kimberley and the greater part of it will answer to him.
suggested_refs: The New Rush diggings on the Colesberg Kopje, renamed Kimberley in 1873
sources: South African History Online, 'Cecil John Rhodes'

stops.name: The Big Hole, the pit and the arithmetic
stops.date_confidence: attested for Frank Rhodes joining the camp in January 1872; the consolidation described runs from here to 1888. Coordinates corrected to the pit itself, one lens having placed it some 700 metres east
stops.campa: The pit widens year by year, the largest hole ever dug by hand, and Rhodes moves through it buying. His brother Frank comes up from Natal to work beside him. He states the logic plainly: fragmented claims flood the market and ruin the price, while one owner can hold the stones back and set it. De Beers Consolidated will in time join the De Beers and Kimberley mines with the Dutoitspan and Bultfontein interests, and a mineral once dug for by the barrow becomes an administered scarcity.
suggested_refs: The Kimberley Mine, the Big Hole, worked 1871-1914
sources: Rob Turrell, Capital and Labour on the Kimberley Diamond Fields 1871-1890

stops.name: Bechuanaland, the trek after the first attack
stops.date_confidence: attested that a heart attack in mid-1872 stopped him working for nearly eight months and that he then trekked north through Bechuanaland and the Transvaal; the route is not documented and this pin marks the Bechuanaland leg generically
stops.campa: At nineteen his heart fails him for the first time and he cannot work for nearly eight months. The convalescence he chooses is a trek by ox wagon north through Bechuanaland and the Transvaal, months in open country with a companion and no fixed purpose. He comes back to Kimberley with his health mended and with the road north measured under his own wheels, hundreds of miles of grass with no European power sitting on it. He will spend the next thirty years taking it.
suggested_refs: The wagon roads north from Kimberley through Bechuanaland to the Transvaal, 1872
sources: South African History Online, 'Cecil John Rhodes'

segments.name: Oriel and the Confession of Faith

stops.name: Oriel College, matriculation in fragments
stops.date_confidence: attested; the geography and afterlife lenses give slightly different coordinates for Oriel, 51.7505/-1.2529 and 51.7519/-1.2528, and the divergence is recorded rather than resolved
stops.campa: He is admitted to Oriel and keeps terms in fragments, sailing back to the diamond fields between them. His mother dies and his own chest drives him south again; he is in Kimberley by January 1874, working the claims through a slump in the fields while his name stays on the college books. Oxford for him is not an education but a membership, taken in instalments over eight years alongside a fortune made three thousand miles away. He will remember the dons as men who had governed nothing and had opinions about everything.
suggested_refs: Oriel College buttery books and matriculation registers, 1873-1881
sources: South African History Online, 'Cecil John Rhodes'

stops.name: Oriel College, the second residence
stops.date_confidence: attested for the return to Oxford in 1876; the term is not specified in the reachable sources and the date defaults to the year
stops.campa: He returns to Oriel for a further term, a man of twenty-two who already owns mines, and goes on keeping terms in fragments until 1881. The two halves of the life settle into place here. The money is made in Africa and the meaning is manufactured in England. He crosses between them by steamer, a digger among dons and a don among diggers, at ease in neither and using both. The college will still be arguing about him a hundred and forty years after he stops paying his battels.
suggested_refs: Oriel College, Oxford, and the intermittent residence of 1873-1881
sources: South African History Online, 'Cecil John Rhodes'

stops.name: Oxford, the Confession of Faith and the Apollo Lodge
stops.date_confidence: the Confession of Faith is dated 1877 and the Masonic initiation to June 1877; the lodge's meeting place in that year is not pinned in the sources reached, and the coordinate marks central Oxford rather than a documented address
stops.campa: In his rooms he writes out a private paper he calls a Confession of Faith. It asks why, the English being the finest race, they should not take the whole habitable globe, and answers itself with a proposal: a secret society modelled on the Jesuits, funded by the accumulated wealth of the like-minded, to bring the uncivilised world under British rule and recover the United States. In the same season he is initiated into the Apollo University Lodge. He is twenty-three and has written down the programme of his next twenty-five years.
stops.quote: I contend that we are the first race in the world, and that the more of the world we inhabit the better it is for the human race.
stops.quote_source: Cecil Rhodes, Confession of Faith (1877), printed in W. T. Stead, The Last Will and Testament of Cecil Rhodes (1902), Part II, Chapter I
suggested_refs: The manuscript Confession of Faith, printed in full by Stead in 1902
Apollo University Lodge No. 357, Oxford
sources: Stead, The Last Will and Testament of Cecil Rhodes (Wikisource edition)
South African History Online, 'Cecil John Rhodes'

stops.name: Kimberley, the De Beers Mining Company floated
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; Rotberg dates the float to April 1880 and the month is not independently confirmed here
stops.campa: Rhodes and Charles Rudd float the De Beers Mining Company on the claims they have spent nine years accumulating. It is the vehicle rather than the destination. Over the next eight years it will absorb its rivals one by one, until a single board decides how many stones reach Europe in a year and at what price. Rhodes is twenty-six and has not finished at Oxford. He has understood before his competitors that a diamond is worth whatever a monopoly says it is worth.
suggested_refs: The 1880 prospectus of the De Beers Mining Company Limited
sources: Turrell, Capital and Labour on the Kimberley Diamond Fields

stops.name: Cape Town, the seat for Barkly West
stops.date_confidence: attested that he was elected for Barkly West in 1880 and took his seat in 1881; South African History Online gives his age as 29, which is wrong, he was 27, and Wikipedia gives 27
stops.campa: He takes his seat in the Cape House of Assembly as member for Barkly West, elected the previous year at twenty-seven. He will hold the seat without a break until he dies, through premiership, disgrace, and war. The Cape parliament of these years runs a colour-blind franchise on a property qualification, English and Dutch members bargaining across a floor on which a small number of Black and coloured voters count. Rhodes enters it as a mine owner who needs laws, and leaves it as the man who rewrote the qualification twice.
suggested_refs: Debates of the Cape House of Assembly, 1881 session
sources: South African History Online, 'Cecil John Rhodes'

stops.name: Barkly West, the constituency that never turns
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; he held the seat continuously from 1881 to 1902 and this pin stands for the whole tenure rather than a dated visit
stops.campa: The constituency itself is river diggings and dust, alluvial claims on the Vaal, a mostly Black district and an electorate that is not. He courts the Dutch farmers in their own idiom and they return him for twenty-one years, including the elections after the Jameson Raid, when the rest of the colony will not forgive him. Barkly West is the one piece of ground loyal to him from the beginning to the end, and he keeps its name at the head of his letters after he has lost every other office.
suggested_refs: The alluvial river diggings of Barkly West on the Vaal

stops.name: Kuruman, the Warren Expedition on the missionaries' road
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Warren Expedition marched from the Cape in the early months of 1885 and passed through Bechuanaland; the month at Kuruman itself is a reconstruction
stops.campa: The road north runs through Bechuanaland, and Boer freebooters have set two small republics across it while Germany feels along the coast to the west. Rhodes lobbies London until it moves. Sir Charles Warren's expedition marches up the missionaries' road past the station at Kuruman and takes the country without a battle. Rhodes calls the corridor the Suez Canal into the interior; whoever holds it can reach the Zambezi, and whoever does not is shut into the southern tip of the continent for good.
suggested_refs: The London Missionary Society station at Kuruman and the road north it opened

stops.name: Vryburg, the corridor secured
stops.date_confidence: the Protectorate was declared 31 March 1885 and British Bechuanaland became a separate Crown colony in September 1885; one research lens dated the whole business to 1884, which belongs to the lobbying rather than to the act
stops.campa: The Bechuanaland Protectorate is declared at the end of March, and in September the southern portion becomes the Crown colony of British Bechuanaland with Vryburg for its capital, a town a Boer republic had proclaimed for itself three years before. The corridor is open. Rhodes has secured with other men's soldiers and the imperial treasury's money a road he intends to use privately. The Crown takes the ground first; the charter will come from the Crown afterwards.
suggested_refs: The proclamation of the Bechuanaland Protectorate, 31 March 1885
sources: South African History Online, 'Cecil John Rhodes'

stops.name: New Court, the money in St Swithin's Lane
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the Rothschild financing of the De Beers amalgamation and of the chartered company is attested, the dates of particular meetings at New Court are not
stops.campa: He comes to New Court in St Swithin's Lane, and the money that will amalgamate the diamond fields is arranged across a table in the City. N M Rothschild and Sons finances the De Beers consolidation and stands behind the chartered company that follows. African ground is taken from here on by companies capitalised in London, governed by boards in London, and reported to shareholders in London, while the men who dig it are paid in compounds five thousand miles from the register of members.
suggested_refs: N M Rothschild and Sons, New Court, St Swithin's Lane, London

stops.name: Kimberley, De Beers Consolidated Mines
stops.date_confidence: sources diverge: Wikipedia gives 13 March 1888 for the founding, South African History Online gives April 1888 for the formal formation; the divergence is left standing and the earlier date used for ordering
stops.campa: De Beers Consolidated Mines is registered, and its trust deed is written wider than any mining company requires: power to annex territory, to raise armies, to govern. The monopoly is complete, the world's rough passes through one office, and the profits are earmarked from the first day for something other than diamonds. Rhodes is chairman at thirty-four. He has built a private revenue that answers to no parliament, and he is about to spend it on a country that does not yet have a name.
suggested_refs: The trust deed of De Beers Consolidated Mines Limited, 1888
sources: South African History Online, 'Cecil John Rhodes'

stops.name: Bulawayo, the Rudd Concession signed
stops.date_confidence: attested to 30 October 1888 at Bulawayo; South African History Online's March 1888 is an error and is rejected rather than hedged. The coordinate is the site of Lobengula's later Bulawayo, near the modern city; one lens placed the kraal more than a degree of latitude too far north
stops.campa: At Lobengula's Bulawayo, Charles Rudd, James Rochfort Maguire, and Francis Thompson obtain from the Ndebele king a document granting complete and exclusive charge over all the metals and minerals in his kingdoms, in return for rifles, cartridges, a steamboat on the Zambezi, and a hundred pounds a month. The king is told that nothing will follow but a few men digging a hole. Within a year the paper is in London being read as the title to a country. Lobengula repudiates it and no one in London listens.
suggested_refs: The Rudd Concession, 30 October 1888, and Lobengula's letters repudiating it
sources: South African History Online, 'Cecil John Rhodes'

stops.name: Downing Street, the royal charter
stops.date_confidence: attested to 29 October 1889 by South African History Online; Wikipedia gives the year without the day
stops.campa: The royal charter of the British South Africa Company is granted, empowering a private company to govern, police, and exploit the country from the Limpopo to the great lakes on the strength of the Rudd paper. The chartered company is an old English instrument turned to a new use. The Sierra Leone Company at Freetown, which Robert Finley took as his working model when he proposed Liberia in 1816, was the same device aimed at settlement rather than extraction. Rhodes is thirty-six, and the company he has founded is now a government.
suggested_refs: The Royal Charter of the British South Africa Company, 29 October 1889
sources: South African History Online, 'Cecil John Rhodes'

stops.name: Macloutsie, the Pioneer Column musters
stops.date_confidence: attested; the column set out from Macloutsie on 28 June 1890 and crossed the Tuli on 11 July. Coordinates corrected: one lens placed the camp south of the Limpopo inside present-day South Africa, whereas Macloutsie lay on the Motloutse river in the Bechuanaland Protectorate
stops.campa: On the Macloutsie river the Pioneer Column musters and sets out on the twenty-eighth of June: a few hundred selected settlers and a larger body of company police, with wagons and guns, privately raised and privately paid. They are not an army, and the fiction matters, because a chartered company may occupy an empty country but may not invade a kingdom. They cross the Tuli in July and march north through the winter grass, keeping wide of the Ndebele heartland, into a Mashonaland whose people are not consulted.
suggested_refs: Camp Macloutsie on the Motloutse river, mustering ground of the Pioneer Column

stops.name: Cape Town, sworn in as Prime Minister
stops.date_confidence: attested; Wikipedia gives 1890 broadly, South African History Online July 1890, Rotberg the seventeenth
stops.campa: He is sworn in as Prime Minister of the Cape Colony at thirty-seven, holding at the same moment the premiership of a self-governing colony, the chairmanship of De Beers, and the chartered company that is at that hour marching an armed column into a kingdom eight hundred miles to the north. Nobody in Cape Town considers the combination improper. He governs on Dutch votes as much as English ones, and tells anyone who asks that South Africa cannot be held against the Dutch, a doctrine he will destroy with his own hands.
stops.quote: you cannot govern South Africa by trampling on the Dutch.
stops.quote_source: Cecil Rhodes to W. T. Stead, quoted in Stead, The Last Will and Testament of Cecil Rhodes (1902), Part II, Chapter II
suggested_refs: Government House, Cape Town, and the first Rhodes ministry, 1890-1893
sources: Stead, The Last Will and Testament of Cecil Rhodes (Wikisource edition)
South African History Online, 'Cecil John Rhodes'

stops.name: Fort Salisbury, the flag on the veld
stops.date_confidence: attested; the column halted at the site on 12 September 1890 and the flag was hoisted the following morning, 13 September. One lens dated the dispatch of the column to 13 September, conflating the departure with the flag-raising
stops.campa: The column halts on the twelfth of September beneath a granite kopje, and the flag goes up the following morning; the settlement is named for the Prime Minister in London. Rhodes is not present. He is in Cape Town governing a colony, and the country being taken in his name he has never seen. The pioneers are paid in land and mining claims rather than in money, and within a year they are riding out onto farms already occupied by people nobody asked. The gold is not there in the quantities the prospectus promised.
suggested_refs: The kopje at Fort Salisbury and the flag-raising of 13 September 1890
sources: South African History Online, 'Cecil John Rhodes'

stops.name: Bulawayo, the royal town burned
stops.date_confidence: attested for November 1893; the coordinate is the site of Lobengula's later Bulawayo near the modern city, and the lens value of -19.15 is rejected as roughly 110 kilometres too far north. Old Bulawayo, the earlier royal town, lies further south at -20.3023, 28.6264
stops.campa: Three years of pressure end in war. Company columns with machine guns break the Ndebele regiments in two engagements, and when the troopers reach the royal town in November they find it burned and the king gone north. Lobengula dies in flight within weeks and his grave is never found. The kingdom that granted the concession is dismantled by the company the concession created, and its cattle and its land are handed to the men who rode up with the column. Thirty-four troopers of the Shangani Patrol are cut off and killed.
suggested_refs: The burned royal town of Bulawayo, November 1893; the Shangani Patrol

stops.name: Bulawayo, the new town and the name Rhodesia
stops.date_confidence: the new town dates from 1894 and the official renaming of Zambesia to Rhodesia from May 1895; the month of the town's founding is a reconstruction
stops.campa: A colonial town is laid out on the ashes of the Ndebele capital, its streets cut wide enough to turn a wagon and its span of oxen, and the company administration for Matabeleland sits down in it. The following May the whole territory between the Limpopo and the Zambezi, until then called Zambesia, is officially renamed Rhodesia. A man of forty-one has a country named after him in his lifetime by a company he owns, and the name will stand for eighty-five years, nearly twice as long as he himself lives.
suggested_refs: The 1894 layout of colonial Bulawayo; the renaming of Zambesia as Rhodesia, May 1895

stops.name: Cape Town, the franchise and the Glen Grey Act
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Franchise and Ballot Act is dated 1892 without a month in the reachable sources, and the Glen Grey speech to 27 July 1894, the Act becoming law in August
stops.campa: Twice he narrows the Cape franchise from the inside. The Franchise and Ballot Act raises the property qualification from twenty-five pounds to seventy-five, cutting the Black electorate of a colour-blind constitution. Two years later he rises to introduce the Glen Grey Act: individual land tenure to break communal holding, and a labour tax on any man who has not worked outside his district. In Natal, ashore one year, a Gujarati lawyer named Mohandas Gandhi drafts the first petitions of the Natal Indian Congress the month after.
suggested_refs: The Glen Grey Act, 1894, and Rhodes's speech introducing it, 27 July 1894
sources: South African History Online, 'Cecil John Rhodes'

stops.name: Great Zimbabwe, the ruins given to strangers
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; Rhodes's funding of early excavation and his backing of the foreign-builder theory are attested, but his personal visit is asserted only in later company-era accounts and is not documented to any date
stops.campa: Stone walls stand in the veld, dry-laid without mortar, and Rhodes pays for men to dig them out. The conclusion is settled before the spades go in: Phoenicians, Sabaeans, the queen of Sheba, anyone at all except the Shona whose ancestors built them. The digging is destructive and much of the evidence goes out with the soil. Twentieth-century archaeology will overturn the whole account, and the ruins will give the country its name at independence, but for now the stones are made to testify that Africans build nothing.
suggested_refs: Peter Garlake, Great Zimbabwe (1973), on the dismantling of the foreign-builder theory

stops.name: Pitsani Potlugo, the raid rides out
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: From a company police camp on the Bechuanaland border, Leander Starr Jameson rides for the Transvaal with a mounted column, expecting a rising of Uitlanders in Johannesburg to come out and meet him. The rising does not happen. The column is surrounded and surrenders within days. Rhodes has armed it, paid for it, and provided the ground it starts from. Twenty-five years of building, the premiership, the Dutch alliance, the charter, the reputation, are staked on a private raid into a neighbouring republic and lost inside a week.
suggested_refs: The BSAC police camp at Pitsani Potlugo and the Jameson Raid, 29 December 1895
sources: South African History Online, 'Cecil John Rhodes'

stops.name: Cape Town, the resignation
stops.date_confidence: the premiership formally ended 12 January 1896, Sprigg taking office the next day; one research lens dated the resignation to 6 January, which at most marks the day he tendered it, and the two dates are recorded rather than merged
stops.campa: He resigns the premiership, his complicity in the raid plain, and gives up the headship of the chartered company; he keeps Barkly West. The Cape Dutch he had courted for fifteen years will not deal with him again, and the road to a war between Britain and the republics stands open. Mark Twain, lecturing his way around the world to pay his creditors, is in South Africa in these months and writes the raid up with contempt for everyone in it. He can admire Rhodes and want him hanged in the same paragraph.
stops.quote: But even their wisdom has its limits, and they will hang Mr. Rhodes if they ever catch him. That will round him and complete him and make him a saint. He has already been called by all other titles that symbolize human grandeur, and he ought to rise to this one, the grandest of all.
stops.quote_source: Mark Twain, Following the Equator (1897), Chapter LXVIII
suggested_refs: Mark Twain, Following the Equator (1897), chapters on Rhodes and the Jameson Raid
sources: Wikipedia, 'Prime Minister of the Cape Colony'
Mark Twain, Following the Equator (Project Gutenberg etext 2895)

stops.name: Matobo Hills, the indaba
stops.date_confidence: the indabas in the Matobo Hills in August 1896 are attested; the detail that Rhodes walked in unarmed rests on Flint and the tradition around him and is carried as reconstruction
stops.campa: The Ndebele rise, and the Shona with them, and the company's police are away in the Transvaal as prisoners. Settlers die by the hundred and Africans by far more in the risings the country will remember as the Umvukela and the first Chimurenga. Rhodes goes north out of office, appoints himself a colonel, and then does the thing that will be told of him longest: he rides into the Matobo Hills with a handful of companions and sits down on the ground among the indunas to talk. The war ends without a further campaign.
suggested_refs: The Matobo indabas of August and September 1896

stops.name: Malindidzimu, the grave chosen
stops.date_confidence: attested that he chose the site during the 1896 peace talks; the month is a reconstruction. Coordinates corrected: two lenses placed Malindidzimu some 5.7 kilometres south-southwest of its actual position
stops.campa: Between the sittings he rides up onto a granite dome the Ndebele call Malindidzimu, the place of benevolent spirits, and decides to be buried there. The hills hold the shrines of Mwari, though the principal one stands at Njelele, a different hill, and the distinction is lost in most of what is written afterwards. He calls the summit the View of the World, and puts it in his will: a grave cut into bare rock in a country carrying his name, thirty-five kilometres from the capital of the kingdom he broke.
stops.quote: I admire the grandeur and loneliness of the Matoppos in Rhodesia and therefore I desire to be buried in the Matoppos on the hill which I used to visit and which I called the 'View of the World'
stops.quote_source: Cecil Rhodes, Last Will and Testament, 1 July 1899, in Stead, The Last Will and Testament of Cecil Rhodes (1902), Part I
suggested_refs: Malindidzimu, World's View, Matobo Hills
sources: Stead, The Last Will and Testament of Cecil Rhodes (Wikisource edition)

stops.name: Westminster, Committee Room 15
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the Select Committee on the raid sat in 1897 and Rhodes gave evidence to it, but the room and the month are not confirmed against a primary record here
stops.campa: A Select Committee of the Commons sits on the raid and Rhodes gives evidence. He declines to produce the telegrams that would show what the Colonial Secretary knew, and the committee censures him without stripping him of anything that matters. Joseph Chamberlain, who signs the censure, keeps his office. The verdict is arranged in advance by men who want the raid condemned and the expansion continued, and Rhodes walks out of it damaged in England and still sovereign north of the Limpopo.
suggested_refs: Report of the Select Committee on British South Africa, 1897

stops.name: Victoria Falls, the line and the bridge
stops.date_confidence: disputed; the railway and telegraph scheme is attested and the bridge was completed in 1905, after his death, but whether Rhodes ever stood at the falls is a persistent tradition with no dated primary account behind it, and the year here is nominal
stops.campa: The Cape to Cairo scheme is a railway and a telegraph line running the length of the continent through British territory, and the falls sit on its route. He orders the bridge built where the spray will fall on the carriages, and does not live to see it; the span is thrown across the gorge in 1905. Whether he ever stood at the falls himself no dated account establishes. The scheme is a map coloured before it is surveyed, and its author is dying of the heart he was sent to Africa to save.
stops.quote: I would annex the planets if I could; I often think of that. It makes me sad to see them so clear and yet so far.
stops.quote_source: Cecil Rhodes to W. T. Stead, quoted in Stead, The Last Will and Testament of Cecil Rhodes (1902), Part III
suggested_refs: The Victoria Falls Bridge, opened 1905, built to Rhodes's instruction that the spray reach the carriages
sources: Stead, The Last Will and Testament of Cecil Rhodes (Wikisource edition)

stops.name: Cairo, the terminus he never reached
stops.date_confidence: no source places Rhodes in Egypt; the visit is legend rather than record and the pin marks the northern terminus of the scheme, not a journey. The date is nominal and is recorded as a gap
stops.campa: Cairo is the northern end of the line on the map, and there is no record that Rhodes ever went there. No biography places him in Egypt; the visit is a tradition without a document, and it is set down here as a gap. What is real is the line itself, drawn from the Cape through country he owns, country he intends to own, and country belonging to Belgians, Germans, and Ottomans who have not agreed to any of it. He annexes on paper faster than any expedition can walk.
stops.quote: The world is nearly all parcelled out, and what there is left of it is being divided up, conquered, and colonised.
stops.quote_source: Cecil Rhodes to W. T. Stead, quoted in Stead, The Last Will and Testament of Cecil Rhodes (1902), Part III
suggested_refs: The Cape to Cairo railway and telegraph project, mapped 1890s
sources: Stead, The Last Will and Testament of Cecil Rhodes (Wikisource edition)

stops.name: Groote Schuur, the will signed
stops.date_confidence: attested; the main will is dated 1 July 1899 with codicils running to March 1902, and it was probated after his death. One research lens dated the will itself to 1902, which is the probate year
stops.campa: At the Dutch house he bought under Devil's Peak in 1893, burned in 1896 and rebuilt for him by Herbert Baker, he signs a will he has been rewriting since he was twenty-four. The early versions left everything to a secret society. This one endows scholarships at Oxford for young men from the colonies and the United States, and by a later codicil from Germany, so that those who govern the English-speaking world will have been formed in one place. He leaves the house to the nation for its prime ministers.
stops.quote: No Student shall be qualified or disqualified for election to a Scholarship on account of his race or religious opinions
stops.quote_source: Cecil Rhodes, Last Will and Testament, 1 July 1899, in Stead, The Last Will and Testament of Cecil Rhodes (1902), Part I
suggested_refs: Groote Schuur, Rondebosch, rebuilt by Herbert Baker after the 1896 fire
The Rhodes will of 1 July 1899 and its codicils
sources: Stead, The Last Will and Testament of Cecil Rhodes (Wikisource edition)

stops.name: Kimberley, inside the siege
stops.date_confidence: attested that he was in Kimberley through the siege of October 1899 to February 1900; the day of his arrival is a reconstruction
stops.campa: War comes as he had made likely, and he goes up to Kimberley by rail and stays inside the town through four months of siege. De Beers feeds the population, sinks shelters in its own mine shafts, and builds a gun in its workshops. He quarrels continuously with the garrison commander over relief and over who shall shelter where. The town he assembled claim by claim is now his fortress, and a heart that has been failing since he was nineteen is asked to sit out a bombardment.
suggested_refs: The siege of Kimberley, 14 October 1899 to 15 February 1900, and the De Beers workshops

stops.name: Muizenberg, the cottage by the sea
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date, place, age and cause; the coordinates are corrected to Rhodes Cottage on Main Road, two research lenses having placed it between 1.1 and 1.5 kilometres away
stops.campa: He comes down to a small rented cottage at Muizenberg for the sea air, as he was sent out to Africa for air at sixteen, and dies there of heart failure at forty-eight. The autumn is hot; they cut a vent in the wall behind his bed and pack ice about the room. He is unmarried and childless. He leaves a country carrying his name, a company holding the world's diamonds, a scholarship not yet founded, and thirty-two years in Africa. The last codicil to the will is signed in the same month.
stops.quote: So much to do, so little done!
stops.quote_source: Cecil Rhodes, dying words, 26 March 1902, recorded in Stead, The Last Will and Testament of Cecil Rhodes (1902), Part III
suggested_refs: Rhodes Cottage, Main Road, Muizenberg, now a museum
sources: Stead, The Last Will and Testament of Cecil Rhodes (Wikisource edition)

stops.name: Cape Town, lying in state
stops.date_confidence: attested that the body lay in state in the Houses of Parliament before the funeral of 3 April; the exact days are not pinned in the sources reached. One research lens placed the lying in state in St George's Cathedral, which is where the service was held, and the two locations are separated here
stops.campa: The body is brought to the Houses of Parliament and lies in state in the building where he sat for twenty-one years and rewrote the franchise twice. Cape Town files past, Dutch and English together, the quarrel of the raid suspended for the length of a funeral. He has been out of office six years and out of favour for most of them, and the crowd is enormous anyway. The colony is at war with the republics while he lies there, in a war his own raid did much to bring on.
suggested_refs: The Houses of Parliament, Cape Town, where Rhodes lay in state, April 1902

stops.name: St George's Cathedral, the funeral
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The funeral service is held at St George's and the procession goes down Adderley Street between crowds to the station. Guns fire in salute. The colonial government, the company, the mining houses, and the imperial garrison walk behind him, and so do men from the Matabeleland campaigns. Then the coffin is put on a train and sent north, out of the colony he governed and into the country named for him, along the railway he built for other freight entirely.
suggested_refs: St George's Cathedral, Cape Town, funeral service of 3 April 1902

stops.name: Malindidzimu, the burial and the royal salute
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date and for the salute; coordinates corrected as at the 1896 stop
stops.campa: The train runs north for a week through Kimberley, where the town turns out to file past the funeral car, and up to Bulawayo. Oxen drag the coffin the last thirty-five kilometres into the hills. He is lowered into a grave cut in the granite of Malindidzimu under a plain brass plate, and the Ndebele indunas present give him the royal salute, Bayete, said to be the first time it was offered to a white man. Jameson will be buried beside him, and the thirty-four of the Shangani Patrol lie a short walk off.
stops.quote: I admire him, I frankly confess it; and when his time comes I shall buy a piece of the rope for a keepsake.
stops.quote_source: Mark Twain, Following the Equator (1897), Chapter LXIX
suggested_refs: The Rhodes grave at World's View, Matobo Hills, and the adjacent Shangani Patrol memorial
sources: Mark Twain, Following the Equator (Project Gutenberg etext 2895)

stops.name: Devil's Peak, the memorial dedicated
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the month of dedication is not given in the reachable sources and defaults to January
stops.campa: A granite temple goes up on the slope of Devil's Peak above the land he left to the nation, designed by Herbert Baker: a stair of forty-nine steps, one for each year he lived, eight bronze lions by John Macallan Swan along it, and the Physical Energy horseman of G. F. Watts at the foot. The bust at the top carries his dedication. In 1929 the British Association meets in South Africa and Margaret Murray sails out to it, one of thousands of visitors taken up this hill to look north along the axis he drew.
stops.quote: To the spirit and life work of Cecil John Rhodes who loved and served South Africa.
stops.quote_source: Inscription, Rhodes Memorial, Devil's Peak, Cape Town
suggested_refs: Rhodes Memorial, Devil's Peak, Herbert Baker 1912

stops.name: Matobo Hills, the demand for the bones
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Independent Zimbabwe leaves the grave where it is. In December 2010 the provincial governor of Bulawayo calls it an insult to African ancestors, and in February 2012 ZANU-PF activists demand that the bones be dug up and returned to Britain. Chief Masuku objects, the archaeologist Godfrey Mahachi objects, and Robert Mugabe, who has spent thirty years unmaking most of what the man built, declines to move him. The grave stays, visited and paid for by tourists, in the hills where the indabas were held.
suggested_refs: The 2010-2012 exhumation debate over the Rhodes grave at World's View

stops.name: Rondebosch, the statue comes down
stops.date_confidence: attested for the removal on 9 April 2015, the day after the council vote; the precipitating protest of March 2015 is widely reported but is carried here as reconstruction
stops.campa: A student throws waste over the bronze figure seated at the top of the university steps, on land Rhodes bequeathed, and the campaign takes his name: Rhodes Must Fall. Within a month the council votes, and the statue is lifted off its plinth by crane in front of a crowd. The plinth is left empty. The movement crosses to Oxford inside the year and turns an argument about a dead man into an argument about whom a university is for, conducted in the two places he paid for.
suggested_refs: The empty plinth on the upper campus of the University of Cape Town

stops.name: Devil's Peak, the nose cut from the bust
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Five months after the statue comes down at the university, someone climbs the memorial on Devil's Peak and cuts the nose from the bust. It is not repaired. The place had been a tea room and a view; it becomes a monument with the argument legible in it. Nothing is added to explain the damage. The memorial keeps its opening hours and its view north along the axis he drew, and the face at the top of the stair is missing a nose. The argument about him is being conducted on the monuments now rather than on paper.
suggested_refs: The defaced bust at Rhodes Memorial, September 2015

stops.name: Oriel College, the statue that stays
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Oxford Union vote of 19 January 2016 and the college announcement of 29 January 2016, and for the 2020 and 2021 decisions described; the Oriel coordinates differ slightly between research lenses and the afterlife value is used here
stops.campa: At Oriel, where he kept broken terms and to which he left his money, a statue of him stands over the High Street. The Oxford Union votes 245 to 212 for removal, and the college announces ten days later that the statue stays, after donors threaten to withdraw gifts and bequests worth more than a hundred million pounds. In 2020 the governing body votes toward removal and appoints an inquiry; in 2021, the inquiry having recommended removal, the college decides against on grounds of cost and planning. Some hundred and fifty academics refuse to teach its students.
suggested_refs: The Rhodes Building, Oriel College, High Street, Oxford, and its statue of 1911
